Was... way more effort that I originally expected, but I like the end result!

The plywood, acrylic, paper, screws, and some wires came from what I had leftover from when I built a DDR pad a little while back. Everything else (buttons, encoders, wires, Ardunio, etc) I bought for as-cheap as possible :p

Button sizes are as-described in the Pancake guide (see part log; 60mm, 33mm, and whatever the FX buttons are). Encoders are 600 P/R optical.

The design was built around the size of the acrylic I had. The bottom board is the same size as the acrylic, and the top board is 0.5cm shorter on all sides so the acrylic goes over it (seemed like a cool idea at the time, and it turned out as-expected). Button and rotary placements are what I assume to be arcade-like (came from the Pancake guide).

Control board is a Leonardo R3 with leovxhq. Buttons, lights, and encoders seem to work fine with it, and I like the LED control modes (reactive and HID; reactive relies on the game to tell the lights what to do and I'm guessing HID just lights the buttons when they're pressed).

Wiring is... a mess (I underestimated the warnings about this), but it works. Everything is hooked directly to the Arduino (through breadboard wires) according to the default pin layout for leovxhq, no resistors involved. The Leonardo R3 has 3 ground pins so I have the encoders sharing one, all the switches sharing one, and all the leds sharing the final one. All the leds can be powered on at the same time seemingly without issue (was concerned about power draw initially).

Encoders were a minor concern, but they seem fine. I only have the shaft going through the acrylic; the small base at the top of the encoder is underneath the acrylic. Basically, the exposed shaft on the top of the acrylic is pretty short. The rotary knobs are barely on the shaft, but they didn't bump off or anything during gameplay. As to how they're mounted; I cut a square into the plywood and the encoder rests through the hole, and the encoder itself is surrounded by sticky tack (got the idea from another user here). Surprisingly it does hold up well :p

FX buttons were also a concern. They're raised higher than the other buttons, and I do notice it while playing, but it's not too bad. I ordered IIDX buttons that'll replace them with at some point, and probably use those two buttons for service and LED mode switch buttons or something.

The wire area is exposed from the front and back, but it could easily be covered with a board or acrylic if I wanted to. The Arduino sits on the top panel which in-hindsight may be a little problematic with the USB cord (the cord will be pulling lightly downward towards the table/surface), so I'll have to figure out something for that.

Total cost was about $70 but that's not including the stuff I had lying around already.

At some point in time I'll throw specific details on measurements, and more detailed instructions on my wiki.
